answer: The guest agent keeps the previous frame for each `(display, session)` pair in memory (`guest/diff.go:18-23`, `guest/diff.go:78-88`), with at most 16 sessions. `changes` splits both frames into 16×16 px tiles and compares each tile row by row with `bytes.Equal` (`guest/diff.go:16`, `guest/diff.go:29-57`). It counts the tiles that differ and merges them into one bounding box, so it returns the changed fraction of tiles plus that box. If there is no previous frame or the screen size changed, the whole screen counts as changed. `diffOp` then crops the current capture to that box, encodes only the crop, and sends no image when nothing changed (`guest/diff.go:90-103`).

The sandbox stores the last frame for each display and session, compares each new capture against it, and returns only the bounding box of what changed plus a cropped image of that box (`server/registry.py:92`). When the guest agent supports it, `diffOp` keeps the previous frame in `lastFrames` (`guest/diff.go:79-87`), and `changes` compares the two frames in tiles, joining the changed tiles into one box (`guest/diff.go:29-47`). If the guest can't do it, the server uses `screen.diff` (`server/screen.py:32`), where Pillow's `ImageChops.difference(...).getbbox()` finds the tightest box around the changed pixels (`server/screen.py:22`). In both paths, a session's first call or a change in screen size marks the whole screen as changed, and an unchanged screen returns `box=None` with no image. One mismatch: `changed` is the share of changed tiles in the guest but the box's share of the screen area on the server, even though the server's docstring says it matches the guest (`server/screen.py:19`).

Login throttling happens in `server/auth_api.py:168-169`. Every `/auth/login` request is checked against two limits: one per client IP, allowing 20 requests per 60 seconds (`server/limits.py:34`), and one per email, allowing 10 per 60 seconds (`server/limits.py:35`). The email check ignores case, as `tests/test_hardening.py:146-152` shows.

Both limits use `Limit.check` (`server/limits.py:15-28`), which keeps an in-memory sliding window of timestamps for each key. Once a key reaches its count, the request gets an HTTP 429 with "too many requests, try again later" and a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds until the oldest attempt expires (`server/limits.py:21-25`). Because these counters live in the process's memory, they reset on restart and aren't shared between server instances. Also, every attempt counts toward the limit, not just failed ones.

Login throttling happens in the `/auth/login` handler: every attempt runs `LOGIN_PER_IP.check(client_ip(request))` and then `LOGIN_PER_EMAIL.check(email)` before the password is checked (`server/auth_api.py:168-169`). The limits are sliding windows that live in memory: 20 attempts a minute per IP and 10 a minute per lowercased email (`server/limits.py:34-35`). Past either limit, `Limit.check` raises HTTP 429 with "too many requests, try again later" and a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds until the oldest attempt leaves the window (`server/limits.py:21-25`). Every attempt counts, including successful logins. Counts are kept separately in each API worker process, and behind a proxy the per-IP limit only works if `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` is set (`server/limits.py:1`, `server/limits.py:41-43`).

When a platform supplies an `edit` callback, `relay.handle` hands off to `stream_edits` (`integrations/relay.py:86-87`). `stream_edits` first sends a "Working…" message, then collects each `action`, `text` and `error` event from the agent's run stream (`integrations/relay.py:95-99`). At most every `EDIT_INTERVAL` (1.2s, `integrations/relay.py:14`), it rewrites that same message with the rendered events plus a trailing "…" (`integrations/relay.py:100-102`). The message is edited one last time when the run ends, or set to "Done." if there were no events (`integrations/relay.py:103`). `render` puts text on plain lines, actions after "›" and errors after "⚠️", and keeps only the end of the text if it's longer than the platform limit (`integrations/relay.py:33-43`). Slack edits with `chat.update` (`integrations/slack.py:81-82`) and Discord with `reply.edit` (`integrations/discord.py:46-47`). WhatsApp can't edit sent messages, so it sends one message per step instead (`integrations/whatsapp.py:1-2`).

When the chat platform supports editing messages, `handle` calls `stream_edits` (`integrations/relay.py:55-91`, branch at `:86-87`). Otherwise it falls back to `stream_messages`, which posts each update as a new message. `stream_edits` first posts a "Working…" placeholder, then reads `run.stream()` and collects the `action`, `text` and `error` events (`integrations/relay.py:94-99`). At most once every `EDIT_INTERVAL` (1.2s, `integrations/relay.py:14`), it rewrites that placeholder with `render(events, limit - 2) + "\n…"`, keeping the text within the platform's length limit (`integrations/relay.py:33`, `:100-102`). When the run finishes, it makes one last edit with the full rendered text, or "Done." if there was nothing to show (`integrations/relay.py:103`).

Container CPU % is worked out from Docker's stats in `server/monitor.py:18-35`. It takes the change in the container's `total_usage` since the previous sample (`cpu_delta`, line 27) and divides it by the change in the host's `system_cpu_usage` over the same interval (`system_delta`, line 28). It returns 0 if either change is zero or negative (line 30). Otherwise the result is `(cpu_delta / system_delta) * online_cpus * 100`, rounded to 2 decimals (line 35), where `online_cpus` falls back to the length of `percpu_usage` and then to 1 (line 33), so a container can show more than 100% when it uses several cores.

The Windows guest agent works it out separately as CPU time divided by elapsed wall time × 100 (`guest/metrics.go:33`).

The `cpu()` helper in `server/monitor.py:17-35` calculates it from a Docker stats snapshot. It takes `cpu_delta`, the change in the container's `cpu_usage.total_usage` between `cpu_stats` and `precpu_stats` (`server/monitor.py:21-27`). It also takes the change in host `system_cpu_usage` over the same interval (`server/monitor.py:24-25`). If either change is zero or less, it returns 0 (`server/monitor.py:30`). Otherwise it returns `(cpu_delta / system_delta) * online_cpus * 100`, rounded to 2 decimals (`server/monitor.py:33-35`); `online_cpus` falls back to the length of `percpu_usage`, or 1. Because of that multiplier, the value can go above 100% on multi-core hosts, so the monitoring page divides it by `host.cpus` for its chart (`web/src/routes/_app/monitoring.tsx:61`).

The custom encoder is `encodePNG` in the Go guest agent (`guest/fastpng.go:14`). `encodeImage` calls it for PNG output at `zlib.BestSpeed` (`guest/screen.go:78`), and `encodeImage` is used both for full screenshots (`guest/screen.go:43`) and for cropped diff regions (`guest/diff.go:98`). The comment at `guest/fastpng.go:12-13` gives two reasons it beats `image/png`: every row uses the cheap Sub filter, which suits the flat runs of color in screenshots, and it compresses with klauspost's deflate (`guest/fastpng.go:9`), which is much faster than the standard library's. It also skips the alpha channel and writes 8-bit RGB (`guest/fastpng.go:22`, `:36-37`), so it compresses 25% less data, and there's a benchmark against `image/png` at `guest/fastpng_test.go:71`.

The custom encoder is `encodePNG` in `guest/fastpng.go:14`. Its only caller is `encodeImage` at `guest/screen.go:78`, which uses it for every screenshot that isn't JPEG, at `zlib.BestSpeed`. According to the doc comment (`guest/fastpng.go:12-13`), it's several times faster than Go's standard `image/png` for two reasons: it applies the cheap "Sub" filter to every row (`guest/fastpng.go:31-37`), which works well on the long flat runs of colour in screenshots, and it compresses with klauspost's deflate, which is much faster than the standard library's. It also always writes plain 8-bit RGB with no alpha channel (`guest/fastpng.go:22`), so there's less data to filter and compress; you can measure the speedup with `BenchmarkStdPNG` and `BenchmarkFastPNG` (`guest/fastpng_test.go:62`, `:71`).

The app signs each AWS KMS request itself with AWS Signature Version 4. It doesn't use an AWS SDK; it calls httpx directly (`server/kms.py:86`). `aws()` reads `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the environment and refuses to run if either is missing. If `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` is set, it adds that as the `x-amz-security-token` header (`server/kms.py:132-144`). `sigv4()` hashes the method, path, sorted headers and payload into a canonical request. It then signs that with a key derived by chained HMAC-SHA256 over date, region, `kms` and `aws4_request`, and returns the `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=…, SignedHeaders=…, Signature=…` header (`server/kms.py:98-128`). That header goes on a POST to `kms.<region>.amazonaws.com` with `x-amz-target: TrentService.Encrypt` or `TrentService.Decrypt` (`server/kms.py:135-148`).

Zoo signs AWS KMS calls itself with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4), using plain `httpx` rather than an AWS SDK. `aws()` reads `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the environment and adds `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` as `x-amz-security-token` when it is set (`server/kms.py:131-144`). `sigv4()` builds a canonical request from the sorted headers and the payload's SHA-256 hash, then signs it with HMAC-SHA256 using a key derived by chaining HMACs over `"AWS4"+secret`, the date, region, `kms` and `aws4_request` (`server/kms.py:98-128`). The result goes in the `Authorization` header of a POST to `https://kms.{region}.amazonaws.com/`, with the region taken from the key's ARN or else `AWS_REGION` (`server/kms.py:89-95`, `server/kms.py:145-148`).

On Linux, outbound traffic is controlled from outside the sandbox. A host-side `zoo-guest -egress DIR` daemon reads one JSON policy per sandbox, so nothing running inside the sandbox can change it (`guest/egress.go:3-8`; the API's side that builds the policy is `server/egress.py:38`). The daemon turns those policies into an nftables ruleset and loads it with `nft -f -` (`guest/egress_linux.go:13-19`, `guest/egress_linux.go:34-41`). A NAT prerouting chain redirects DNS (port 53) to the daemon's own resolver and HTTP/HTTPS (ports 80 and 443) to its filtering proxy on port 15128, which allows or denies each connection by the TLS server name or the Host header (`guest/egress.go:986-988`, `guest/egress.go:462`, `guest/egress.go:523`). For all other traffic, a forward chain accepts established connections, the policy's fixed allow addresses, and a timed set of addresses learned from allowed DNS answers (`a_<tag>`), then rejects the rest when the policy's default is `deny` (`guest/egress.go:1015-1025`, `guest/egress_linux.go:22-31`).

On Linux, a host-side daemon (`zoo-guest -egress DIR`) runs outside every sandbox and enforces each sandbox's JSON policy (`default` allow/deny, a `dns` flag, and domain/ip/cidr rules), so nothing inside the sandbox can change it (`guest/egress.go:3-10`, `guest/egress.go:61-67`). It replaces one nftables table, `inet zoo`, by piping it to `nft -f -` (`guest/egress_linux.go:18-41`, `guest/egress.go:921-936`). For a sandbox that is deny-by-default or has domain rules, a prerouting NAT chain redirects ports 80/443 to a filtering proxy and port 53 to a filtering DNS resolver (`guest/egress.go:967-990`). The proxy allows or denies by the TLS server name or Host header, a deny rule always beats an allow, and loopback, link-local and the host's own addresses stay blocked unless an ip/cidr rule opens them (`guest/egress.go:159-218`, `guest/egress.go:543-582`). All other forwarded traffic goes through a per-sandbox forward chain that rejects denied addresses, accepts allowed ones plus IPs that allowed DNS answers handed out (kept for 30 minutes), and ends in `reject` when the default is deny (`guest/egress.go:993-1027`, `guest/egress.go:812-816`, `guest/egress_linux.go:22-32`).

The API doesn't connect to the port at all. It goes through the zoo guest agent running inside the sandbox, which already holds a connection to the API. On the API side, `Tunnel.open` registers a stream ID and sends a `tunnel_open` call over that connection (`server/guest.py:242-249`); writes go out as `tunnel_write` notifications (`server/guest.py:254-255`). Inside the sandbox, `tunnelOpen` in the guest dials `127.0.0.1:<port>` itself (`guest/tunnel.go:47`), then relays the bytes in both directions as `tunnel_data` frames and ends with a `tunnel_close` frame (`guest/tunnel.go:38`, `guest/tunnel.go:61-70`). The service, for example x11vnc on port 5900, only ever sees a local connection, so its port never has to be published (`guest/tunnel.go:12-13`).

The API never connects to the port itself. It goes through the zoo guest agent, which runs inside the sandbox, over the connection the API already has to that agent (`guest/tunnel.go:12-13`). On the API side, `Tunnel.open` sends a `tunnel_open` call with the port number (`server/guest.py:242-246`). The guest agent then dials `127.0.0.1:<port>` from inside the sandbox (`guest/tunnel.go:47`) and streams the bytes back as `tunnel_data` frames, ending with a `tunnel_close` frame (`guest/tunnel.go:38`). Writes from the API go the other way as `tunnel_write` notifications (`server/guest.py:255`, `guest/tunnel.go:110`). The noVNC proxy uses this to reach x11vnc on its unpublished port 5900 whenever the guest supports tunnels (`server/sandbox_api.py:1000-1001`, `1030-1032`).

`cpu()` in `server/monitor.py:17-35` uses the Docker `docker stats` formula. It subtracts the previous sample from the current one for both the container's `cpu_usage.total_usage` and the host's `system_cpu_usage` (`server/monitor.py:21-28`), returning 0 if either difference is ≤ 0 (`:30-31`). It then computes `(cpu_delta / system_delta) * online_cpus * 100`, falling back to the length of `percpu_usage` (or 1) when `online_cpus` isn't reported (`:33-35`). That means 100% equals one full core, so a container can go above 100%. The monitoring chart divides that number by `host.cpus` to show a share of the whole host (`web/src/routes/_app/monitoring.tsx:61`), and Windows guests calculate it separately as CPU time over elapsed wall time × 100 (`guest/metrics.go:33`).

It uses the same formula as `docker stats`. `cpu()` takes the Docker stats snapshot and finds how much the container's `total_usage` grew since the previous sample (`precpu_stats`), and how much the host's `system_cpu_usage` grew over the same interval (`server/monitor.py:21-28`). If either change is zero or negative, it returns 0.0 (`server/monitor.py:30-31`). Otherwise it returns `(cpu_delta / system_delta) × online_cpus × 100`, rounded to 2 decimals, so a container using several cores can go above 100% (`server/monitor.py:33-35`); the CPU count comes from `online_cpus`, or from the length of `percpu_usage` if that's missing. That value becomes `cpu_percent` (`server/monitor.py:82`), and the monitoring page's chart divides it by the host's CPU count to show 0–100% of the whole host (`web/src/routes/_app/monitoring.tsx:61`).

The code doesn't use boto3. `aws()` reads `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the environment and raises an error if either is missing (`server/kms.py:131-134`). If `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` is set, it also adds that as `x-amz-security-token` (`server/kms.py:143-144`). `sigv4()` then builds a canonical request from the sorted headers and the SHA-256 of the payload, signs it with HMAC-SHA256 using a key derived from date, region, service and `aws4_request` (`server/kms.py:98-102`, `server/kms.py:118-126`), and sends it as the `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` `Authorization` header (`server/kms.py:128`, `server/kms.py:145-148`). Credentials only come from environment variables, so instance roles, IMDS and `~/.aws` profiles aren't supported.

AWS KMS requests are signed by hand with AWS Signature Version 4 (no boto3). The static credentials come from the `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` environment variables, and if either is missing the call fails (`server/kms.py:131-134`). `aws()` builds a JSON POST to `kms.<region>.amazonaws.com` with `x-amz-date` and `x-amz-target: TrentService.<Action>` headers. If `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` is set it's sent as `x-amz-security-token` (`server/kms.py:135-144`), and the request then gets an `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` `Authorization` header from `sigv4()` (`server/kms.py:145-148`). `sigv4()` hashes a canonical request, signs it with an HMAC-SHA256 key derived from the secret over date, region, `kms` and `aws4_request`, and signs every header (`server/kms.py:98-128`). The region comes from the key ARN, or from `AWS_REGION` / `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` if the key isn't an ARN (`server/kms.py:89-95`).

Linux guests are filtered on the host, not inside the sandbox. The `zoo-egress` container runs in the host's network namespace and rewrites one nftables table, `inet zoo`, in a single transaction each time policy changes (`guest/egress_linux.go:13-20`, `guest/egress.go:921-936`). For proxied sandboxes, a prerouting chain sends web traffic (TCP 80/443) to the egress daemon's filtering proxy, and sends DNS to its resolver if the policy allows DNS; the API endpoint and allowed IP ranges skip this redirect (`guest/egress.go:966-989`). A forward chain for each sandbox then decides all other traffic in this order: always-allowed endpoints are accepted, then IPv6 (for proxied sandboxes), DNS (when not allowed), denied ranges and learned-deny addresses are rejected, then established flows, allowed ranges and learned-allow addresses are accepted, and anything left is rejected under a deny-by-default policy (`guest/egress.go:992-1026`). The learned sets get addresses with a timeout as the proxy and DNS resolver make decisions (`guest/egress_linux.go:22-31`), and an input chain keeps the daemon's ports for sandboxes only and blocks deny-by-default sandboxes from reaching anything else on the host (`guest/egress.go:1029-1053`).

On Linux, the sandbox can't touch its own network policy. The server writes a per-sandbox policy file and hands it to a host-side egress daemon, `zoo-guest -egress`, which runs in a container in the host's network namespace with NET_ADMIN (`server/docker.py:299-325`, `server/docker.py:333-350`). That daemon renders the policies into an nftables `inet zoo` table and loads it with `nft -f -` (`guest/egress_linux.go:18-41`, `guest/egress.go:922`). A NAT prerouting chain redirects the sandbox's TCP 80/443 to a filtering proxy, and DNS to its own resolver when DNS is allowed; the proxy decides by the TLS server name or the HTTP Host header (`guest/egress.go:985-988`, `guest/egress.go:462`, `guest/egress.go:523`). All other forwarded traffic goes through a per-policy chain that rejects denied prefixes and learned deny IPs (`d_` set), accepts allowed prefixes and learned allow IPs (`a_` set, with timeouts), and rejects everything else when the default is `deny` (`guest/egress.go:999-1025`, `guest/egress_linux.go:22-32`).

The noVNC desktop path uses this: when the guest supports tunnels, `proxy_tunnel` connects the browser websocket to x11vnc on `VNC_PORT` and handles the VNC login itself (`server/sandbox_api.py:1000-1001`, `server/sandbox_api.py:1030-1066`).

The API goes through the zoo-guest agent's existing connection instead of a published port. On the server, a `Tunnel` (`server/guest.py:229-262`) sends a `tunnel_open` call with the target port, then moves bytes in each direction with `tunnel_write` and `tunnel_data` frames, and ends with `tunnel_close`. Inside the sandbox, the guest handles `tunnel_open` by dialing `127.0.0.1:<port>` itself (`guest/tunnel.go:39-47`), so the service only has to listen on loopback. Desktop sandboxes use this for VNC: Docker leaves port 6080 unpublished when the image has the `zoo.guest.tunnel` label (`server/docker.py:163-189`), and `proxy_tunnel` connects the noVNC websocket to x11vnc on `VNC_PORT` through that tunnel (`server/sandbox_api.py:1000-1001`, `1030-1066`).

On Windows and macOS hosts there's a similar path that uses an SSH `direct-tcpip` channel to `127.0.0.1` instead of the guest (`server/windows.py:341-344`, `server/macos.py:168`).
